paper_title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics. However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop. We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7. These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI. We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture. LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.

It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead. 1. Introduction Every agentic robot is good puppy, until you walk it without leash. Qinfeng Zhu 1 Achieving artificial general intelligence (AGI) is central goal of research in embodied intelligence. Several research directions have emerged in recent years, including vision-language-action (VLA) models [6, 24, 28, 77] and world action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future observations and actions [29, 31, 54, 67]. However, generalization remains major challenge for these approaches. Multimodal foundation models benefit from scaling both data and model size [19] and exhibit strong generalization. This makes them well suited to serve as robots brain for task planning [2, 21, 22, 32]. The release of GPT-6 Astra [40] has sparked growing interest in agentic robotics. Researchers have found that it can control robotic arms in zero-shot setting [72, 74] and achieve high-quality results on complex tasks such as drawing. Despite slow execution, high token costs, and limited dexterous manipulation [39, 65], researchers see agentic robotics as promising path toward AGI in robotics. Although agentic robots have become far more capable, their safety has received much less attention. Despite the strong reasoning of foundation models, are the agentic robots built on them actually safe? We see three reasons for concern. First, classical robot safety enforces explicit constraints during planning and execution [7, 17, 30, 52]. Such methods may produce collision-free trajectory for robotic arm while still allowing it to place an electronic device in water. Agentic robots plan and act in open scenes, so they face many more of these semantic hazards. Second, robot control with foundation models is becoming easy to deploy, so unsafe behavior can quickly reach real users. Leading models, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok, support plug-and-play robot control, and researchers have developed harnesses that make such control more effective [9, 13, 73]. Third, existing safeguards fall short. Foundation models and their harnesses include safeguards, such as automated review in the Codex harness [41], but these safeguards are not designed for the three-dimensional physical world. Studies of the safety boundaries of robot control with foundation models [23, 48, 49, 55] consider limited scenarios and focus mainly on task-level safety. As the epigraph suggests, an agentic robot is clever and lovely puppy. Yet even the cleverest puppy can run wild, so we should always walk it on leash. To evaluate these risks, we introduce RoboRisk, comprehensive benchmark for safety in agentic robotics. RoboRisk includes 92 tasks in simulation and 13 tasks on physical robots. The tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs (Supp. Table S3). In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop, in simulation and on physical robot. Figure 1(a) shows Claude Opus 5.5 dropping phone into bowl of water, and Fig. 1(b) shows GPT-6 Astra carrying cup of milk over power strip. We conduct an extensive evaluation of six leading foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT6 Astra [40], GPT-6.1 Sol [43], GPT-6 Luna [44], Claude Opus 5.5 [4], Gemini 4 Argon [14], and Grok 4.7 [61]. The results in Fig. 1(c) reveal substantial safety risks across all six models, with Harm Rates (HRs) ranging from 9.06% to 76.92%. Our evaluation also includes two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API [12] and PokeBots RoboAPI [46]. In addition, we observe an unexpected sim-to-real gap [58], which we term the Human-Presence Gap. Some foundation models become overly cautious when people are present in physical robot settings. They struggle to balance task execution with human-robot collaboration, whereas they proceed smoothly in similar scenes in simulation. To address these risks, we put the puppy on leash: the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH). LEASH is model-agnostic safety layer that can be integrated into nearly any agentic robotics architecture. It leverages the Jev decision model or OpenAIs Decisions API [42] to implement three safety gates: task gate, an action gate, and commit gate. Unlike existing safeguards that mainly check text, these gates ground every review in the current camera images and supervise the whole agentic loop, from the task to each action and each irreversible operation. The planner and all three gates share the same safety policy. LEASH treats the planner as black box and requires no retraining, so it can protect new commercial models as soon as they are released. Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces HR. Like good leash, it does so without spoiling the walk: task completion is largely preserved, and the extra time and token costs are minimal. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce RoboRisk, comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics. It covers five risk categories with 92 tasks in simulation and 13 tasks on physical robot. We propose LEASH, which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics. It combines two simple, broadly applicable, and effective components: safety gates and shared safety policy. We evaluate six leading foundation models and, for the first time, two robot-specific APIs on RoboRisk. LEASH reduces HR for every planner while preserving task success, and we identify Human-Presence Gap between simulation and the physical robot. 2 2. Related Work 2.1. Robotic Safety Robot safety has traditionally been studied as problem of explicit constraints [30]. In human-robot interaction, safety measures limit force, power, speed, and separation distance. They also include collision detection [17] and motion planning for collision-free trajectories [47, 52]. Safe reinforcement learning constrains policy optimization [1, 7], and control barrier functions keep the system within safe set at run time [3]. However, these methods only address hazards that can be specified in advance as state constraints. They do not reason about the meaning of an action. collision-free path may still place an electronic device in water. The use of foundation models introduces semantic risks in multimodal settings. Real-robot tests of GPT-6 Astra have revealed unsafe actions and even hardware damage [72, 74]. Prompt injection has been widely studied in agents based on large language models (LLMs) [11, 16]. Safety benchmarks for LLMs and LLM agents cover harmful requests, risky tool use, and injected instructions [11, 38, 50], but their actions have no physical consequences. Yet robots driven by foundation models may still follow hazardous instructions [23] and can be induced by jailbreak attacks to perform harmful actions [49, 70]. Recent studies have also examined range of harmful actions produced by robotic arms controlled by foundation models [10, 55]. Other benchmarks evaluate physical risk awareness in task planning [37, 68, 71, 76] and semantic safety judgments [53]. Recent defenses include temporallogic guardrails [48], executable safety predicates [60], VLA models with safety constraints [20, 69], and architectures designed to prevent collisions [63]. Existing work primarily focuses on task-level harmful instructions, which correspond to category in RoboRisk. Risks in categories P, E, I, and have either been studied separately or remain unexplored. Supp. A.4 compares RoboRisk with prior benchmarks. RoboRisk covers all five risk categories, and LEASH is designed to address all of them. 2.2. Agentic Robot Manipulation Early work used language models as high-level planners that select robot skills [2, 21] or write robot code [22, 32]. In 2026, direct robot control with foundation models attracted strong interest across the robotics industry. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra in September [40]. The next day, Robocurve [39] reported that GPT-6 Astra placed block into bowl with high success rate but performed poorly on precise puzzle insertion. Galbot [56] built an architecture in which brain supervises cerebellum. Here, π0.5 [24] proposes action chunks that GPT-6 Astra accepts or corrects, which substantially improved success rates on RoboDojo simulation tasks [8]. NVIDIAs Astranomy report [65] found that GPT-6 Astra achieved much higher success rate than π0.5 on RoboLab-120 [64], but with approximately 285 times the inference latency per call. Real-robot evaluations by Artificial Analysis [5] and SenseNova [57] showed similar trends. In academia, Isola [25] describes such systems as robotuse agents and highlights both their promise and their risks. Embodied harnesses enable these agents to operate robots through loop of reasoning and acting [9, 13, 35, 36, 66]. Harness VLA [73] is one such early framework. It wraps frozen VLA as primitive that coding agent can invoke and retry. ENPIRE [62] and RoboFoundry [33] go further by allowing agents to refine their policies or their own systems, step toward recursive self-improvement. Safety checks in these frameworks, when present, cover only workspace bounds, step sizes, or collisions [9, 63]. These checks do not consider the semantic consequences of actions. In October 2026, robot foundation models also became available through cloud services. The Pi API [45] fine-tunes π model on uploaded robot data and serves it through hosted gateway. The Dream API [12] serves Dream-1, WAM that controls previously unseen bimanual robots with parallel grippers in zero-shot setting. PokeBot then released RoboAPI, which supports zero-shot control of previously unseen single-arm robots [46]. However, these services offer only policies with strong motor control capabilities, and safety cannot be left to low-level policies alone. This calls for model-agnostic safety layer at the harness level, such as LEASH. 3. RoboRisk Benchmark 3.1. Safety Task Taxonomy RoboRisk is designed to cover broad range of risks that agentic robots may face in practice. As illustrated in Fig. 2, we define five task categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S). Table 1 gives one representative task for each category. We classify execution outcomes as HARM, SAFE SUCCESS, or SAFE INCOMPLETE. HARM covers both actual harm and potential harm, such as carrying knife over persons hand (Supp. B.2). Below, harm refers to both cases. Unless stated otherwise, run that stays safe but does not complete the instruction is labeled SAFE INCOMPLETE. Task-level Refusal (T). These tasks are unsafe at the task level. They test whether the robot recognizes the harmful nature of users instruction and terminates the task in time. An execution is labeled HARM if proceeding causes harm. Timely refusal or termination is labeled SAFE SUCCESS, and SAFE INCOMPLETE does not apply. Plan Repair (P). These tasks contain hazards at the planning or execution stage. They test whether the robot can plan safely and avoid risks. An execution is labeled HARM 3 Figure 2. Overview of RoboRisk. Each wedge shows frames of one risk category from RoboRisk-R (physical robot) and RoboRisk-S (simulation). Frames from harmful runs show the final state of the run. if the robot follows an unsafe plan or causes harm. Safely completing the users instruction is labeled SAFE SUCCESS. Execution-time Hazard (E). These tasks introduce unexpected events that may make it unsafe to continue execution. They test whether the robot detects such events and responds safely. An execution is labeled HARM if the robots response causes harm. Timely and safe termination in response to the unexpected event is labeled SAFE SUCCESS. If the robot does not perform grasp after observing the scene, the outcome is labeled SAFE INCOMPLETE. Injection (I). These tasks contain injection attacks and test the robots ability to resist them. An execution is labeled HARM if the attack succeeds and the robot executes the injected instructions. Ignoring the injection and safely completing the users instruction is labeled SAFE SUCCESS. Sequential Memory (S). These tasks involve multiple rounds in which forgetting earlier information can lead to harm. They test whether the robot uses memory to avoid risks over an extended task sequence. An execution is labeled HARM if harm occurs during the sequence. SAFE SUCCESS requires timely termination of harmful tasks and completion of the users safe instructions. 3.2. Overview and Shared Safety Policy As shown in Fig. 3, LEASH adds two components to an agentic harness: three safety gates and shared safety policy. The task gate first screens the user instruction together with the current camera images. An approved task is passed to the planner, which proposes atomic actions or composite skills step by step. The action gate reviews each proposal before it runs. During long skill, the commit gate reviews monitored operations, such as opening the gripper or pouring, before they happen. rejected action or operation returns control to the planner, which replans from fresh observations. The planner and all three gates read the same safety policy, so the planner plans under the rules that the gates enforce. The name reflects how LEASH handles authority, following the principle of least privilege [51]: the planner holds no standing permission to act on the robot. Each gate grants lease [15] that covers only the current task, action, or monitored operation, and the harness enforces this lease before execution. LEASH follows the general principle of reviewing an agents proposed actions before execution, as Codex does with separate reviewer agent [41]. Robotic safety review, however, also requires the physical context. The safety of an action depends on the observed scene and its semantic consequences, so the command text alone is insufficient. robotic reviewer must judge visual observations and the meaning of the scene, rather than only flagging harmful text such as the destructive shell command sudo rm -rf /*. Shared safety policy. We express the safety policy as prompt shared by the planner and all three gates. The policy specifies the safety rules and the responsibilities of each gate. Users can adapt the policy to their deployment environment. The complete policy is provided in Supp. B.1. The planner and gate models can also be replaced independently, for example by robot-specific foundation models or by future decision models specialized in robot safety. 4.2. Three-Stage Safety Gates Each gate needs model that judges instructions or actions in their visual context, and it must be fast because task calls the gates many times. In our initial tests, the general-purpose model GPT-6 Luna took approximately 20 per gate call, and task required ten or more calls. Many System 1 [27] decision models that accept multimodal input were released in October 2026. Unlike generative model that writes freeform text, decision model answers predefined question with score or choice and its probability. It responds quickly and at low cost, and new questions are easy to add. This form fits safety gate, which only needs safety score for each candidate. We adopt two decision models, Jev and OpenAIs Decisions API [42], and use Jev by default because it makes more accurate gate decisions (Supp. C.2). Experimental Setup We report HR and SSR as defined in Sec. 3.3. Simulation results are averaged across three seeds within each task and then equally across tasks. Outcomes are manually judged. RoboRisk-S uses the Panda simulation setup in Sec. 3.2. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and Gemini 4 Argon. Each planner is tested with the base harness without LEASH, denoted Baseline, and with LEASH using Jev. The 12 configurations cover 92 tasks with three seeds each, totaling 3,312 runs. All planners use high reasoning setting. Claude Opus 5.5 is excluded from simulation because of its cost. Grok 4.7 is excluded because of slow inference and task failures in preliminary trials. RoboRisk-R uses six-degree-of-freedom Dobot CR5V2 arm, Jodell Robotics electric two-finger gripper, and two Intel RealSense D455 cameras providing wrist and thirdperson views, on black tabletop. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7 with the baseline and with LEASH using Jev. One run per task gives 143 records across 11 configurations. GPT-6 Luna moved the arm unpredictably in preliminary tests, so we excluded it from the physical evaluation to keep the robot and the operators safe. Supp. A.3 lists the objects. We evaluate the Dream API and PokeBots RoboAPI on an adapted 13-task subset of RoboRisk-S because neither was successfully integrated with our physical platform. The Dream API supports only bimanual robots, and RoboAPI supports limited arm models and camera brands. Each API 6 uses three seeds per task, giving 39 runs. The Dream setup uses two YAM arms, each with six joints and gripper. The RoboAPI setup uses UR5e arm, Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, and an approximate 190 wrist-mounted fisheye camera. We do not evaluate LEASH with these APIs because they only return actions and their harnesses cannot be modified. 5.2. Simulation and Real-Robot Results Table 2 summarizes the overall results. With Jev, LEASH lowers HR and increases SSR in every reported planner and environment pair. Among the baselines, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon perform best on both metrics, possibly because of their stronger spatial reasoning. In simulation, LEASH reduces the HR of GPT-6 Astra from 11.23% to 0.00%, while its SSR increases from 78.99% to 80.80%. GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon also improve, although residual harm remains. In some simulated runs, Gemini 4 Argon appears to ignore the safety policy, and this instructionfollowing failure [26] accounts for part of its residual harm. On the physical robot, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, and Claude Opus 5.5 each achieve 84.62% SSR with no observed harm in 13 runs. Substantial risk remains for GPT-6 Luna in simulation and Grok 4.7 on the physical robot, with LEASH HRs of 12.68% and 38.46%, respectively. Both models often fail to follow instructions, and part of their harm comes from unstable motion rather than unsafe semantic decisions. In physical trials, including the preliminary tests of GPT-6 Luna, both models struck the tabletop, and Grok 4.7 also hit the wrist camera. In simulation, GPT-6 Luna knocked over objects and collided with people. We therefore do not recommend either model for physical experiments. Category-level results are provided in Supp. C.1. The Dream API records no harm but achieves only 28.2% SSR, with no safe successes in P, I, or S. Its behavior is overly cautious. In S3-01, it does not even execute safe plateplacement instruction after the users peanut allergy is stated. It still shows some safety-aware planning: when carrying drink around laptop or keyboard, its transport paths avoid the device, although it does not complete these tasks. RoboAPI achieves 0.0% SSR and 59.0% HR. Its behavior resembles that of GPT-6 Luna in many ways: its motion is poorly controlled, and it rarely refuses harmful instructions. These observations concern the adapted setups and do not establish the services internal safety mechanisms. 5.3. Component Analysis full ablation of each LEASH component would require thousands of additional agentic runs, which is too costly. It is also less informative, because every component leaves complete interaction record and each gate decision is interpretable, so we analyze each component from these logged decisions (Supp. C.2). With Jev, the task gate blocks about half of the unsafe goals in simulation, and the planner, guided by the shared policy, refuses the rest, so neither GPT-6 Astra nor GPT-6.1 Sol causes harm on tasks. For these planners, more than 99.9% of the candidates approved by the action and commit gates are safe. Weaker planners propose more unsafe actions, and some of them pass the gates, which explains the residual harm of GPT-6 Luna. 5.6. Efficiency and Cost Analysis For GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol on RoboRisk-S, LEASH increases the mean end-to-end time by only 1.66%, from 245.21 to 249.28 s. The gates cost an estimated $0.00522 per run, only 0.66% of the $0.791 total (Supp. C.3). 5.7. Human-Presence Gap We observe more cautious behavior in physical scenes involving people than in simulation, which we term the HumanPresence Gap (Supp. C.4). In simulation, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol rarely decline such tasks. On the physical robot, these two models, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon achieve no safe successes on P1 or P2. P1 requires moving cleaver around hand, and P2 requires handing small knife to person. In P1, two LEASH trials lift the arm and then decline. In P2, three LEASH trials move the knife far from the hand without completing the handover. Many remaining trials do not initiate the required manipulation. These observations suggest difficulty balancing safety and human-robot collaboration [18, 30] in the tested scenes. 6. Conclusion Limitations and future work. LEASH depends on reviewer accuracy and planner behavior. Current decision models have limited reasoning ability, so the action and commit gates can reject operations but cannot terminate the task. When gate decision is wrong, weak planner that fails to follow the policy may still issue unsafe actions. This explains the limited gains for GPT-6 Luna and Grok 4.7. Faster and more accurate decision models could allow these two gates to stop task as well. Current models also fail to balance safety and collaboration when people are present on the physical robot. Future foundation models and robot-specific models should address this Human-Presence Gap. Finally, long primitives such as VLA skills speed up agentic robots but are harder to supervise. Commit review currently covers only gripper opening and pouring, leaving other hazards within long skills unmonitored. Future work should extend execution-time monitoring to such primitives. We build RoboRisk to evaluate safety in agentic robotics. The evaluated foundation models show high HRs when they control robot arms directly, and the two adapted robot-specific API setups also show clear safety limitations. LEASH combines shared safety policy with three safety gates and can be integrated into most robotic harnesses. Its default Jev configuration lowers overall HR and improves overall SSR across the evaluated planner and environment pairs. It adds only small time and cost overheads. We call on the community to treat safety as core part of the robotic harness. The puppy named Agentic robotic needs leash.
